query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled ~3 at.% oxygen content during the processing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs) that trap oxygen internally, thereby enhancing the alloy’s high-temperature oxidation resistance without compromising its yield strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast, oxygen-lean equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with known poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 3 atomic percent oxygen into the alloy during melting/casting (via controlled oxygen doping) to enable OOC formation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at 1000 °C in an oxidizing (air) atmosphere for around 100 hours; mechanical performance evaluated under tensile loading at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs) dispersed within the single-phase bcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen atoms preferentially occupy interstitial sites associated with (Hf, Ti)-rich chemical short-range orderings, forming coherent OOCs. These complexes trap oxygen internally, providing interstitial solid-solution hardening while preventing deleterious oxygen segregation (especially at grain boundaries), thus maintaining ductility and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxygen-doped alloy is expected to exhibit significantly reduced high-temperature oxidation (evidenced by lower oxidation weight gain) while retaining or even modestly enhancing the yield strength and ductility compared to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which shows poor oxygen resistance along with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Valid within the processing conditions of controlled oxygen doping during cast alloy production; performance assessed at 1000 °C in air for prolonged exposure (∼100 hours) with tensile testing conducted at strain rates from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: While the concept of OOC formation via controlled oxygen doping has been validated in similar bcc systems (e.g., Ti–Zr–Nb alloys), its direct transferability to HfNbTaTiZr is uncertain and may be influenced by differences in elemental interactions and phase stability that could affect oxygen solubility and segregation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr: one with a controlled ~3 at.% oxygen addition during casting and one untreated control. Subject both sets of samples to an oxidation test at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. After exposure, perform tensile tests under strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹ and conduct microstructural analyses (using TEM/SEM) to detect the presence of OOCs and any signs of oxygen segregation, particularly at grain boundaries.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation resistance
Tensile stress-strain curves to assess yield strength and ductility
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM, possibly with EDS) to confirm the presence or absence of OOCs and detect oxygen segregation patterns
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped alloy does not show a significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., oxidation weight gain comparable to or greater than the untreated alloy) or if its tensile properties (yield strength and ductility) are degraded (or if microstructural examination fails to identify coherent OOC formation), then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Oxygen solute strengthening is an effective strategy to harden alloys, yet, it often deteriorates the ductility. Ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs), a state between random interstitials and oxides, can simultaneously enhance strength and ductility in high-entropy alloys. However, whether this particular strengthening mechanism holds in other alloys and how these OOCs are tailored remain unclear. Herein, we demonstrate that OOCs can be obtained in bcc (body-centered-cubic) Ti-Zr-Nb medium-entropy alloys via adjusting the content of Nb and oxygen. Decreasing the phase stability enhances the degree of (Ti, Zr)-rich chemical short-range orderings, and then favors formation of OOCs after doping oxygen. Moreover, the number density of OOCs increases with oxygen contents in a given alloy, but adding excessive oxygen (>3.0 at.%) causes grain boundary segregation. Consequently, the tensile yield strength is enhanced by ~75% and ductility is substantially improved by ~164% with addition of 3.0 at.% O in the Ti-30Zr-14Nb MEA. Ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs) endow a unique interstitial strengthening mechanism for simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility in HEAs. Here, the authors demonstra

The loss of ductility might originate from suppression of the martensite phase transformation or/and twin formation, as reported previously in some dual-phase titanium alloys,,. In the alloys with a given amount of Nb from 14 to 30 at.%, the yield strength increases with the oxygen content (Fig. 1c), demonstrating strong interstitial strengthening. For the ductility wise, when the Nb content is below 26 at.%, it increases with the oxygen concentration (i.e., the ductility change ratio of the doped MEA to the un-doped counterpart is positive) and reaches its maximum in the sample with 3.0 at.% oxygen (Fig. 1d). It is interesting to note that the strongest ductilization effect of oxygen was realized in the alloy with 14 at.% Nb, i.e., with addition of 3 at.% oxygen, the ductility is increased by 164 %.

As described above, the oxygen content also affects the formation of OOCs. Figure 3g, h shows internal-friction spectra (at 1.0 Hz) of the alloys with 14 at.% Nb but a different amount of 1 and 3 at.% O, i.e., Ti–30Zr–14Nb–1O and Ti–30Zr–14Nb–3O. After the peak decomposition analysis, it is known that the ratio of oxygen atoms participating in forming OOCs increases with the oxygen concentration, i.e., from ~14.5% to ~40.9% as the oxygen content is raised from 1 to 3 at.%. As such, the number density of the clusters increases substantially from 1.04 × 1024 m−3 for Ti–30Zr–14Nb–1O MEA (Fig. 3i) to 8.7 × 1024 m−3 for Ti–30Zr–14Nb–3O MEA (Fig. 3j). Moreover, in the low oxygen-doped Ti–30Zr–14Nb–1O MEA (see Supplementary Fig. 6e, f), fewer oxygen atomic columns were observed in the interstitial sites within light-atom-rich regions, indicating a reduction in the amount of OOCs with the decrease of doped O content. With the further increase of oxygen, i.e., the Ti–30Zr–14Nb–4O MEA, the 6.8 at.%-O iso-composition surfaces and the corresponding 1D concentration map also reveal the occurrence of grain boundary segregation of oxygen (Fig. 3k1, k2).

Additionally, no oxygen segregation at grain boundaries was observed for the Ti–30Zr–14Nb–3O (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Fig. 13a, b) and Ti–30Zr–30Nb–2O MEAs (Fig. 5i and Supplementary Fig. 13c, d). Nevertheless, O segregation at grain boundaries did occur in Ti–30Zr–14Nb–4O (Figs. 3k1, k2, 5g) and Ti–30Zr–30Nb–3O MEAs (Figs. 3f1, f2, 5j), despite that no oxide was formed in both MEAs (Supplementary Fig. 14a, b). As a result, the fracture mode changed from ductile fracture (predominantly dimpled rupture) to intergranular brittle fracture mode in these two MEAs (Supplementary Fig. 14c–f). Therefore, the solid solubility of O atoms in the current MEAs decreases with the increase of Nb, which is consistent with the DFT calculations that the O solubility for Ti-30Zr-14Nb is higher than that for Ti-30Zr-30Nb MEA. Consequently, grain boundary embrittlement resulted from oxygen segregation is responsible for the premature fracture behavior and low ductility in the Ti-30Zr-14Nb-4O and Ti-30Zr-30Nb-3O MEAs. Our approach is based on the creation of OOCs via promoting the formation of (Ti, Zr)-enriched CSROs, and the unique interstitial strengthening effects from OOCs simultaneously realized

reading.lever: Introduce precisely ~3 at.% oxygen into HfNbTaTiZr to promote OOC formation, trapping oxygen and improving oxidation resistance.
reading.why: This approach, proven in similar bcc alloys, can control oxygen interactions without sacrificing strength or ductility in the targeted system.
